Learning Objectives
Identify signs of malunion.
Discuss the differences between malunions and deformities at fracture sites.
Explain the appropriate evaluation of deformities.
Review treatment options for malunions and deformities at fracture sites.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Malunions result from the incorrect healing and alignment of fractures.
Malunions can occur in fractures managed surgically or nonsurgically.
No inherent, predictable relationship exists between angulation and translation. The
translation that occurs at the site of a malunion may be compensatory or contributory to the
angular deformity as it relates to the mechanical axis of a limb.

The distinction between a malunion and a mild deformity at a fracture site remains vague, and
no absolute guidelines exist.

Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
A malunion results from a fracture that heals in a nonanatomic position to a degree that
it impairs function or becomes symptomatic. A malunion can cause symptoms of pain or
disability via asymmetric loading of an adjacent joint, resulting in increased contact
pressure, overloading ligaments, muscle/tendon irritation, tension strain on the bone,
and impairment of normal ambulation or motion.1-6 A malunion also can result from
bony union with associated shortening, translation, angulation, rotational malalignment,
or a combined deformity.
Accurate characterization of the malunion regarding location, severity, and direction is
required to identify the most effective treatment option. The position of the distal
segment relative to the proximal segment is used to describe the direction of the
deformity. Lower extremity malunions tend to be more symptomatic than upper
extremity malunions because length discrepancy and asymmetric joint loading are
affected by body weight, thereby magnifying the effects of the malunion. Upper
extremity malunions may be more clinically important in patients with paraplegia, who
may rely on the upper extremities for ambulation, or patients with specific occupational
dependence on upper extremity function. Most patients with upper extremity deformity
after a fracture can compensate because of the forgiving mobility of the shoulder joint.
Symptoms present quickly if the deformity interferes with gait mechanics, and the
compensatory capacity of adjacent joints is overwhelmed. An example is if a
procurvatum deformity of the femur interferes with a patient’s ability to lock the knee
during the stance phase of gait or while standing.7 Most symptoms resulting from
malunions occur more gradually because of asymmetric adjacent joint contact pressure
and subsequent pain.1-3,5,6

Osteology
Upper Extremities
Shortening is better tolerated in the upper extremity than in the lower extremity.
Proximal humerus
The proximal humerus has little constraint; large deformities are tolerable, except the
tuberosities, in which smaller displacements may result in impingement and shoulder pain.
Diaphyseal humerus
Angular deformities of as much as 30° may be tolerated by the humeral shaft.
Sagittal plane deformities are better tolerated than coronal plane deformities because they
are in the plane of motion.
Angular deformities at the supracondylar level are more poorly tolerated because of an
altered carrying angle. These are limited to 10° of valgus and, occasionally, as much as 15° of
varus.
Forearm
Small translational and angular deformities are poorly tolerated because they interfere with
pronation and supination.
Isolated shortening of the radius or ulna of more than 3 to 5 mm also is poorly tolerated
because of altered wrist mechanics.
Lower Extremities
Shortening of more than 2 cm in the lower extremity represents a malunion in the axial plane.
Angular malunions about the knee and ankle of 10° or more in the coronal plane are poorly
tolerated and may require correction.
Some data suggest that more than 5° of malalignment may lead to hip or knee arthrosis.
Management should be individualized.
Angular and translation deformities in the sagittal plane are better tolerated because the axis
of motion of the knee and ankle is in the sagittal plane.
Rotational malalignment of more than 15° is considered problematic; however, smaller
amounts of malrotation may be poorly tolerated and require correction. With any translational
deformity, especially in the tibia, a coexisting rotational deformity usually is present.

Patient History
Open versus closed fracture
Surgical history, laboratory studies, cultures
Current functional status

Patient History
Accurate evaluation of a malunion begins with a thorough medical history, including the
nature and timing of the initial injury and all treatment performed between the initial
treatment and the current presentation. Soft-tissue status (open or closed initial injury,
whether soft-tissue coverage was required, whether infection or draining sinus is
present) along with the patient’s current functional status and the location of pain
should be documented. The level of supportive resources and the patient’s overall
motivation/insight also should be considered because gradual correction requires good
compliance and consistent follow-up. The patient should be queried about the location
and type of symptoms related to the malunion.
Physical Examination
Neurovascular examination—Any preexisting deficits must be documented, and vascular
compromise may affect management.
Range of motion of all adjacent joints—Angular or rotational deformity may result in stiffness
or laxity of adjacent joints; this must be considered in planning for possible correction.
Rotational profiles—Although often neglected in the workup, failure to address rotational
deformity may result in major deficits after correction of an angular deformity. A gunsight CT
scan generally aids in evaluating rotational deformity of the lower extremity. Most rotational
deformities are subtle and detected only via a careful clinical examination of the hips, knees,
and ankles.

Physical Examination

During the physical examination, a neurovascular examination and assessment of the
range of motion for joints adjacent to the malunion should be performed. Range of
motion, or lack thereof, of an adjacent joint may affect treatment decisions. If an
adjacent joint has a rigid compensatory deformity, then correction of the malunion will
result in a secondary deformity at the level of the joint. For example, with a distal tibia
valgus malunion, the subtalar joint may partially compensate for the tibial deformity.8
The mobility of the subtalar joint should be assessed to determine if it has the flexibility
to return to a normal position after the malunion is corrected to avoid varus
malalignment at the level of the subtalar joint. A fixed varus position of the foot will
result if the subtalar joint is not flexible (Figure 1). The malunion site should be stressed
to assess the stability of union and for the presence of pain. If pain is present, additional
imaging studies may be helpful to rule out a nonunion, which may alter management.
Gait abnormalities and rotational alignment of the femur and tibia should be
documented.

Because of concerns about soft tissue in the area of the previous fracture site, patient
evaluation is critical. A history of open fracture, soft-tissue coverage, and infection are
factors that should be considered during the preoperative assessment. Although
correction may ideally occur at the level of the deformity, compromised soft tissue at the

level of the previous fracture site may require that the osteotomy be made at a location
farther away from the deformity than preferred.
The patient must have a good understanding of the treatment plan, including the
duration of treatment and the possibility of failure. A solidly healed malunion may
become an unstable or infected nonunion after osteotomy, which may result in
amputation. The patient should be aware of these types of risks and be willing to
proceed before treatment is initiated. In patients with medical comorbidities (diabetes
mellitus, smoking history, malnourishment), optimization strategies should be
implemented before treatment to increase the likelihood of successful surgical
treatment.
Imaging Studies
Evaluation of mechanical axis deviation via a standing long-leg radiograph is required to
accurately understand lower extremity deformity or malunion.
Mechanical Axis

Mechanical Axis
The femoral mechanical axis is identified by a line drawn from the center of the femoral
head down to the center of the knee joint. The tibial mechanical axis is identified by
drawing a line from the center of the knee joint down to the center of the ankle joint. The
mechanical axis of a bone is always a straight line because it always connects two points.
The mechanical axis of the tibia is slightly lateral to the mid-diaphyseal line/anatomic
axis (Figure 2).

Figure 2 Drawings show the axes of the femur and tibia. A, The mechanical axis of the
femur and tibia is determined by drawing a line from the center of the femoral head to
the center of the knee joint and from the center of the knee joint to the center of the
ankle joint. B, The anatomic axis of the femur and tibia is determined by drawing a line
through the midpoint of two lines drawn perpendicular to the long axis of the bone
spanning from both cortices. This resultant line connecting the midpoints represents the
anatomic axis, which is collinear with the medullary canal. The tibial anatomic axis is
straight on the frontal and sagittal planes, whereas the femoral anatomic axis is straight
on the frontal plane but varies on the sagittal plane because of the femoral bow.
(Reproduced from Swanson E: Malunions, in Ricci WM, Ostrum RF, eds: Orthopaedic

Anatomic Axis

Anatomic Axis
The anatomic axis of a bone is identified by a line drawn through the center of the
diaphysis along the length of the bone. Several points along the diaphysis can be
identified by a line drawn perpendicular to the long axis of the bone spanning from
cortex to cortex. This line is then bisected, and this center point is connected for two or
more points along the length of the bone to identify the anatomic axis of the bone. In
the femur, the anatomic axis exits proximally through the piriformis fossa and distally at
the lateral aspect of the medial femoral condyle on an AP view. Depending on the shape
of the bone, the anatomic axis may be straight, as observed on an AP view of the femur,
or curved, as observed on a lateral view of the femur. The tibial anatomic axis is straight
on the frontal and sagittal planes (Figure 2). A summary of joint orientation angles is
shown in Figure 3.

Joint Orientation Angles

Joint Orientation Angles
The intersection of joint orientation lines (Figure 3) and the mechanical or anatomic axis
of the bone in question allows for calculation of the respective joint orientation angles
(Figure 4). Joint orientation angles can be used to determine axis alignment of a bone if
the segment is too short to use the anatomic or mechanical axis lines. In most instances,
a natural template for normal is already provided in the unaffected limb. If both limbs
are affected, the mean value for the population sample is the next best option9 (Table
1). The same convention should be used in assessing alignment: the anatomic axis or the
mechanical axis should be used, but not both, in assessing alignment of a malunited
fracture.

Limb Alignment

Limb Alignment
Full-length, 51-inch bilateral AP standing radiographs obtained with both feet pointed
straight forward and full-length, weight-bearing lateral radiographs of each lower
extremity, showing the hip, knee, and ankle with the limb in full extension, allow for
assessment of limb alignment by drawing a line from the center of the femoral head to
the center of the ankle joint. Mechanical axis deviation refers to the distance from the
center of the knee joint to a line drawn from the center of the femoral head to the center

mm medial to the knee joint center (Figure 4, D).
Center of Rotation of Angulation

Center of Rotation of Angulation
The center of rotational angle (CORA) is the intersection of the proximal and distal bone
segment axes (Figure 5). In the process of deformity correction, the bone may be
rotated around this point to correct angular deformity. Anatomic or mechanical axes
may be used to determine the CORA; however, axis types should not be mixed.
Anatomic axes are easier to use for diaphyseal segments. For periarticular segments,
axis lines can be created by measuring joint orientation angles in the patient’s
contralateral limb or by using mean values from Table 1 to determine the mechanical or
anatomic axis relative to the joint orientation line.

Figure 5 Drawings of the tibia and fibula show the center of rotational angle (CORA),
which is the intersection of the proximal and distal bone segment axes. A, The bisector
line is drawn passing through the CORA and dividing the medial and lateral angles,
creating a transverse bisector line. B, Any point on this transverse bisector line is
considered to be a CORA because rotation about any point on the bisector line will result
in angular correction without secondary translation. (Reproduced from Swanson E:
Malunions, in Ricci WM, Ostrum RF, eds: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Trauma, ed 5.
Rosemont, IL, American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2016, pp 109-129.)
For multi-apical deformities, the anatomic axes should be used for the femur because
assessment of the mechanical axis for a central diaphyseal segment is difficult if the
proximal or distal joint segment is not attached to that diaphyseal segment. To
determine the CORA, a line is drawn along the axes of the segments in question. If these
lines intersect at the level of obvious deformity, then the deformity is uni-atypical. If the
lines intersect outside the bone, a second CORA, or a translational component, exists
(Figure 6). Two angles are created at the CORA. These can be labeled as proximal, distal,
medial, and lateral. In the example shown in Figure 5, the proximal and distal angles are
equal to each other and represent the magnitude of angular deformity. The medial and
lateral angles also are equal to each other. The bisector line is drawn, passing through
the CORA and dividing these medial and lateral angles, creating a transverse bisector
line. Any point on this transverse bisector line is considered a CORA because rotation
about any point on the bisector line will result in angular correction without secondary
translation. Ideally, correction of angular deformity is done at the CORA; however, if soft
tissue, poor bone healing potential, or internal fixation construct options prevent placing
the osteotomy at the level of the CORA and an angular correction must be done
proximal or distal to the CORA, a translational deformity will occur. Often, this
translational deformity is clinically unimportant; however, this predictable result of an
osteotomy not centered at the CORA should be recognized.

Correction Axis

Correction Axis

The correction axis, which is observed if angular correction rotates or pivots to correct
deformity, depends on the location and type of osteotomy performed. Deformity
correction with an osteotomy results in realignment via angular correction alone if the
correction axis lies on the CORA/bisector line, realignment via angular and translational
correction if the correction axis lies on the CORA/bisector line but the osteotomy is away
from the CORA, or angular correction with residual translational deformity if the
correction axis is away from the CORA/bisector line.8,9
Deformity Types

Deformity Types
Deformities are described in terms of direction and magnitude using the position of the
distal segment relative to the proximal segment. Identification of the CORA is essential in
correction of angular deformities. Angulation is characterized by type
(flexion/extension/varus/valgus) and magnitude and whether the mechanical axis or
mechanical axis deviation has any effect. If an angular deformity appears on the frontal
and sagittal planes with the CORA at the same level, then an oblique deformity exists. If
the CORA is at a different level on AP and lateral radiographs, then a translational
deformity also exists. Determination of angular deformity also can be visualized via
three-dimensional CT reconstruction images. If more than one CORA exists on the AP or
lateral view, then a multi-apical deformity exists (Figure 6). Malunions affecting length
include fractures healed in a shortened position, such as in the presence of bone loss or
bayonet apposition of the fracture fragments. Fractures healed in an over-distracted
position result in a malunion with excessive length. Both shortened and distracted
malunions will result in a relative length discrepancy. The evaluation of length deformity
is made via 51-inch bilateral, full-length weight-bearing radiographs or via a CT scan.
Length deformities are described by their direction and magnitude, are measured from
the joint centers, and are compared with the contralateral extremity. If malunion occurs
in the lower extremity, then shortening the longer limb or lengthening the relatively
shortened limb is an option. Care must be taken to distinguish between shortened
malunion and congenital length discrepancy.

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6004091

A limb that has been shortened because of a malunited fracture has neurovascular
structures that were equal in length to the uninjured side at one point, whereas a limb
with a congenital length discrepancies has neurovascular structures that always were
short. This may affect the plan of acute versus gradual length correction and the
magnitude of correction for congenital length discrepancies. Shortening can be
performed acutely as much as the surrounding soft tissues will tolerate. Acute
lengthening of as much as 2 cm has been described to be safe.8,9
Lengthening of more than 2 cm should be performed gradually to avoid an increased
risk of neurovascular injury. Chronic valgus malunions about the knee also should be
considered because correction of valgus alignment may result in neurovascular injury if
performed too quickly secondary to stretch of the peroneal nerve with acute varus
correction.
Rotational malunions are described in terms of the distal segment relative to the
proximal segment and occur about the longitudinal axis of the bone. Magnitude
(degrees) and direction (internal or external) are noted and compared with that of the
unaffected side. Rotational malunion of the femur is the most common malunion of long
bones of the lower extremity, usually occurring after intramedullary nailing.8 Assessment
of rotational deformity may be done clinically10 and radiographically.8,11-13
Malrotation of the femur can be assessed clinically by having the patient lie prone with
the knees flexed to 90°. The femur is passively internally and externally rotated, and the
degree of rotation of the tibia is noted and compared with that of the unaffected side.
The relative difference indicates the magnitude of femoral rotational deformity. This
technique assumes that both tibiae are straight. If an angular deformity of the tibia
exists, it must be factored into the respective degree of internal/external rotation noted.
Tibial rotational deformity also can be assessed with the patient in this position by
measuring the axis of the second ray of the foot with the axis of the femur (Figure 7).

Figure 7 Drawings show clinical assessment of malrotation of the femur, which can be

The femur is passively internally and externally rotated, and the degree of rotation of the
tibia is noted and compared with that of the unaffected side. The relative difference

WM, Ostrum RF, eds: Orthopaedic Knowledge Update: Trauma, ed 5. Rosemont, IL,
American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons, 2016, pp 109-129.)
Another option to clinically assess rotational deformity of the tibia requires the patient to
stand with both patellae facing directly anterior. The axis of the second ray of the foot is
compared in terms of its rotational relationship with the patella or the tibial tubercle.
Any difference represents a tibial rotational deformity. Rotational deformity also can be
evaluated via CT or radiography.8,10,14,15
CT can be used to measure the angle of the femoral neck in relation to the condylar axis
of the distal femur to assess femoral rotational deformity. The relationship between the
proximal tibia and the distal tibia can be evaluated on the same CT scan by comparing
the axis of the proximal tibia with that of the distal tibia/fibula joint (Figure 8).

Depending on the type of deformity and related factors (angulation, length, translation,

neurovascular structures are located on the concave side of a deformity (eg, a valgus
deformity about the knee), acute correction may cause neurovascular injury. Gradual
correction can be performed via a tensioned small wire ring fixator (Ilizarov/Taylor
spatial frame). Malunions with shortened, angulated, or combined deformities often are
best managed via gradual correction with the use of a tensioned small wire ring fixator.
Ideally, osteotomies are made at the level of the CORA; however, osteotomy type and
location may be influenced by deformity type and fixation options for the proposed
method of correction and biologic factors, such as bone and soft-tissue quality. If these
factors result in the osteotomy being made away from the CORA, then the original

deformity may occur (Figure 10). Correction of acute deformity generally is well
tolerated in the femur and humerus because of a forgiving soft-tissue envelope, whereas
the tibial soft-tissue envelope is less forgiving and usually better managed via gradual

Indications
After functional impairment in the appropriate host has been identified, surgical planning can
commence.
Preoperative Planning
After a malunion is identified, planning for surgical correction can begin.
The CORA can be identified using the mechanical axis of each segment of bone.
Osteotomy
Osteotomy along a line bisecting the CORA will result in angular correction.
Osteotomy away from the CORA will result in translation and angular correction.
Various osteotomy techniques, including opening wedge, closing wedge, dome, or single
plane, may be considered and result in satisfactory correction of a given deformity.
Selection of an osteotomy technique and the use of internal fixation or external fixation will
depend on the degree of deformity, patient activity, and the status of the soft-tissue
envelope.
Three concepts are associated with osteotomy for the management of malunion.8
The first concept is that if the osteotomy and angular correction axis pass through any of the
CORAs (any point on the CORA bisector line), then realignment occurs without translation. This
can be achieved via an opening or closing wedge osteotomy (Figure 10, A).
The second concept is that if the correction axis is through the CORA but the osteotomy is at a
different level, then the axis will realign via angulation and translation at the osteotomy site
(Figure 10, B).
The third concept is that if the osteotomy and correction axis are at a level above or below the
CORA, then a translational deformity will occur (Figure 10, C).

Wedge Osteotomy
This osteotomy can be made at the CORA along the bisector line. If the correction axis is
on the convex side, a wedge is resected along the entire bone diameter so the cortices
proximal and distal to the wedge resected on the concave side of the deformity are
compressed. This results in shortening equal to one-half the base of the resected wedge
(Figure 11). If the axis of correction is on the convex side of the deformity, angular
correction results in an opening wedge. The osteotomy traverses the entire diameter of
the bone, and angular correction adds length equal to one-half the base of the opening
wedge created. One technique is to place parallel Kirschner wires proximal and distal to
the osteotomy site. The magnitude of correction is easily measured by the angulation
created between the previously parallel wires. If the axis of correction is central, then a
smaller wedge that spans one-half the diameter of the bone is resected on the convex
side and placed into the opening wedge defect created on the concave side. This results
in a neutral wedge osteotomy, which does not change length. A wedge osteotomy may
be useful for angular deformities with or without minor length deformity. If the axis of
correction lies on the bisector line at the level of the CORA, then alignment of the
anatomic axis can be restored.

Dome Osteotomy

Dome Osteotomy
This type of osteotomy obviates the need for wedge resection and does not create a
large bony void, which requires bone graft, as observed with an opening wedge
osteotomy. A dome osteotomy allows for good bony opposition for healing. A more
accurate description of the dome is one-half of a cylinder rather than a hemisphere,
which would be a true dome. A dome osteotomy allows for angular correction around a
specific axis. If the axis of correction is at the CORA, then alignment without translation
can be achieved; however, if the dome osteotomy goes through the CORA, then a
secondary translational deformity will occur because the axis of correction cannot be at
the point of the osteotomy (Figure 12). If the axis of correction is on the bisector line of
the CORA, then angular correction can be achieved without secondary translational
deformity. Similar to wedge osteotomies, if the axis of correction is on the concave side
of the deformity, some shortening and possible symptomatic overhanging bone will
occur (Figure 13). If the axis of correction is on the convex side of the deformity, then
length is gained; however, the bony contact is diminished and may require bone graft. A
dome osteotomy with the axis of correction centered on the CORA will result in no
change in length with good bony contact and correction of angular deformity without
secondary translational deformity. To avoid translation, the axis of correction should fall
on the CORA/bisector line. If the osteotomy is through the CORA/bisector line, then the
axis of rotation will be proximal or distal to the CORA and will reliably result in a
translational deformity.

Transverse Osteotomy
Transverse osteotomies can be made to correct rotational or translational malunions.
Rotational malunion osteotomies can be made with the use of an intramedullary saw
and exchange nail. Alternatively, an open osteotomy can be made, with plate or external
fixation after rotational correction. Application of a tensioned wire ring fixator with
software correction guidance may allow for precise correction of rotational deformity in
the acute setting (temporarily used intraoperatively) or in the gradual correction setting.
The osteotomy is made after the frame is applied, and strut adjustment can accurately
correct the deformity, which some consider more precise than the parallel Kirschner
wire technique. This procedure often is performed to correct a rotational deformity after
a fracture initially managed with the use of an intramedullary nail with rotational
malreduction. One of the most common complications of this type of osteotomy is
nonunion.18 Because the osteotomy usually is performed in hard diaphyseal cortical
bone, surgeons must avoid thermal necrosis, which can occur with the use of an
oscillating saw. The use of a sharp blade with copious irrigation is recommended to
reduce the risk of thermal necrosis; another method involves the use of a sharp drill bit
and osteotomy completion with the use of an osteotome.
Oblique Osteotomy
Oblique osteotomies correct translational deformities if gaining length is desired and can also
be used to correct combined deformities, including angular and rotational components.

Management Based on Deformity Location

Management Based on Deformity Location
In general, deformity location may influence the type of osteotomy and fixation
construct. Deformities in the diaphyseal region generally have relatively smaller-
diameter cortical bone segments, which allow angular and translational deformities to
be easily observed on radiographs. In the diaphyseal region, correction of angular
deformities can be reliably achieved via wedge osteotomies through the CORA/bisector
line. Intramedullary fixation can aid in the maintenance of alignment by realigning the
medullary canal, which is essentially equivalent to the anatomic axis for the proximal
and distal segments. The load-sharing characteristics of intramedullary fixation make it a
good option for acute correction in diaphyseal bone; however, plate-and-screw or
external fixation constructs also can be used. For deformities occurring closer to the
joint in the metaphyseal or epiphyseal region, correction and fixation may be difficult. In
patients with a periarticular deformity joint orientation angles often are required to
properly identify and characterize the deformity; these angles can be calculated by
imaging the unaffected limb or based on population-generated means (Table 1).
Proximity to the joint also may limit options for osteotomy or fixation. Ligamentous
attachments, tendon origins/insertions, and neurovascular anatomy may limit surgeon
ability to perform correction at the level of the deformity, potentially requiring the
osteotomy/correction axis to be at a point other than the CORA/bisector line. In addition,
limited bone stock in the periarticular region may limit fixation construct options.
Anatomic plate-and-screw constructs and blade plates can be used for periarticular
fixation if acute correction is performed, whereas a tensioned small wire ring fixator is
extremity versatile in achieving fixation in small periarticular bone segments and can be
used for acute and gradual correction.

Acetabular malunions may manifest as pain related to joint incongruity and can be

total hip arthroplasty if posttraumatic arthritis is advanced.19,35,36 Pelvic ring malunions

origin, sitting imbalance, or gait abnormalities resulting from relative lower extremity

or reconstruction.

A plate-and-screw construct is advantageous because of its utility in periarticular
locations and its ability to provide rigid fixation with the potential for interfragmentary
compression. Disadvantages include the requirement for extensive soft-tissue dissection
and restricted early weight bearing. A periarticular anatomically contoured locking
plating is particularly useful for small bone segments close to the joint, possibly
excluding intramedullary fixation as an option.
Intramedullary Nail

Intramedullary Nail
Intramedullary nails have optimal load-sharing characteristics and can help restore
intramedullary alignment, which helps correct angular and translational deformity.
These qualities make intramedullary nails ideal for acute correction of lower extremity
diaphyseal or meta-diaphyseal malunions, whereas use is limited in periarticular
malunions.

Tensioned Small Wire Ring Fixator
A tensioned small wire ring fixator or Ilizarov techniques allow for versatility in the
management of angular, length, rotational, translational, or any combination of these
deformities.8,9,39-43 Advantages of the Ilizarov technique are outlined in Table 2. The
primary disadvantage of this technique is patient inconvenience; the frame usually is left
in place for months, and consistent patient compliance and regular follow-up are
required.

Distraction Osteogenesis
In patients in whom restoration of length is required, distraction osteogenesis is a useful
technique because the patient can bear weight throughout the process, no bone grafting
is required, and substantial length corrections can be made.39,42,44-47 Distraction causes
cell proliferation, bone generation via intramembranous osteogenesis, and vascular
proliferation via a tension-stress effect. After corticotomy (which is different from
osteotomy) and lengthening, a substantial increase in blood flow has been

documented.48,49 To minimize necrosis at the corticotomy site, a low-energy osteotomy
technique, such as a Gigli wire saw, should be used or drill holes should be made
followed by the use of osteotome without completely disrupting the intramedullary
canal/intraosseous blood supply. Ideally, distraction osteogenesis is performed at the
metaphyseal or meta-diaphyseal region because bone regenerate formation is more
robust in these regions. Given that these frames may be left in place for months or years
in extreme cases, surgeons must consider the long-term stability of the construct and
that good frame application techniques are followed. Although techniques vary among
experts in this area of orthopaedic surgery, a latency period of 1 to 3 weeks is
recommended before distraction to allow for the beginning of regenerate formation.
Because the formation of bone is different in every patient, surgeons should monitor
and progress at a rate suitable to each patient. The rate of distraction for a healthy high
school student will differ from that for an individual aged 65 years who has diabetes
mellitus and a suboptimal vascular status. Usually, a rate of 1 mm per day is a good
starting point; this can be modified depending on the regenerate observed on follow-up
radiographs. Most patients require approximately two to three times the amount of time
required for the distraction phase to allow for solid consolidation of the regenerate. This
requires the regenerate to reestablish a cortex and regenerate hypertrophy, which
occurs with weight transfer through the regenerate segment. This is allowed by the
trampoline effect of the tensioned wire construct. Foreshortened hypertrophic
nonunions also can be managed via distraction osteogenesis.49,50 Current systems allow
for complex combined deformities to be simultaneously corrected with the use of
telescopic struts. The Taylor spatial frame is the most widely used version of this type of
tensioned small wire ring fixator; however, other systems are available. A Taylor spatial
frame involves the use of a software program to guide deformity correction.43,51-58 The
deformity can be corrected by placing ring segments perpendicular to the proximal and
distal bone segments that are gradually adjusted to achieve parallel rings and realigned
bone segments. Any residual deformity can be accounted for during the deformity
correction process. Each patient must be approached with respect to his or her unique
deformity, soft-tissue status, physiologic healing potential, and regenerate formation
capacity.

Accurate assessment of a malunion via physical examination and imaging studies is critical for
successful management.
An understanding of the principal components of the clinical and radiographic evaluation of
malunions, including assessment of deformity type, is important to guide management.
Osteotomy type, gradual or acute correction, and internal or external fixation are crucial
factors related to the treatment strategy and must be individualized based on the patient,
deformity location and severity, and surrounding soft-tissue envelope.
